questions.stem: Two annotators label the same 200 images and agree on 72% of instances. What should you conclude?
choices: One annotator is careless; retrain them
The task definition is ambiguous — model performance is capped near the level of annotator agreement, so the guideline needs sharpening before more labelling
The dataset is too small
The model will resolve the ambiguity
questions.explanation: Inter-annotator agreement is an upper bound on achievable measured performance: where humans disagree, the ground truth itself is noise. Measuring it early and rewriting the guideline is far cheaper than discovering the ceiling after training. Blaming an annotator mistakes a specification problem for a diligence problem.

questions.stem: Which TWO belong in an annotation guideline for a detection task?
choices: A rule for partially occluded objects — for example, label if more than a stated fraction is visible
Whether to include or exclude ambiguous edge cases such as reflections, posters and screens showing the object
The model architecture to be used
The learning rate
questions.explanation: Guidelines exist to make independent annotators produce the same labels. Occlusion and depiction-versus-reality are the two decisions that most often go unstated and produce silent inconsistency. Training configuration has nothing to do with what the ground truth means.

questions.stem: Frames extracted from 50 videos are split randomly into train and validation. Validation accuracy is 96% but production accuracy is 71%. Why?
choices: The model is underfitting
Near-identical frames from the same video appear on both sides of the split, so validation measures recall of almost-seen images; the split must be grouped by video
Validation set is too small
The learning rate was too high
questions.explanation: Adjacent video frames are near-duplicates. A random split puts them in both partitions, so the model is evaluated on images it has effectively already seen. Grouping by video, patient, site or session is essential wherever samples share a source.

questions.stem: What does a precision-recall curve show that a single F1 score does not?
choices: The model's speed
Performance across every confidence threshold, so you can choose an operating point rather than accept one
The number of classes
The training loss
questions.explanation: F1 reports one point on the curve, implicitly weighting precision and recall equally. The full curve shows the trade available — whether recall can be raised cheaply, or whether precision collapses immediately past a point — which is the information a deployment decision needs.

questions.stem: Why is a ROC curve often misleading for a heavily imbalanced detection problem?
choices: ROC cannot be computed for detection
The false-positive rate is normalised by a huge number of negatives, so even many false positives barely move it; a precision-recall curve exposes the problem
ROC requires balanced classes to compute
ROC only works for binary problems
questions.explanation: With a million background regions and a hundred objects, a thousand false positives is a false-positive rate of 0.001 — a nearly perfect-looking ROC — while precision is a catastrophic 9%. Precision divides by predicted positives rather than all negatives, which is why it stays informative under imbalance.

questions.stem: Overall accuracy is 91% and stable across releases, but users report the model got worse. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Users are mistaken
Aggregate accuracy is masking a regression in a subset that matters — a class, a site, a lighting condition — that is small in the data but significant in use
The metric is computed incorrectly
The test set is too large
questions.explanation: An aggregate over a fixed distribution can stay flat while an important slice degrades, especially if that slice is rare in the test set but common in a particular user's experience. Per-class and per-segment reporting is what reveals it; a single headline number structurally cannot.

questions.stem: Which TWO slices should be reported separately rather than folded into an overall number?
choices: Performance on rare but high-consequence classes
Performance by capture condition — camera, site, lighting, time of day
Performance grouped by file size
Performance by annotation date
questions.explanation: Consequence and capture condition both correspond to real risk boundaries: a rare critical class needs its own threshold, and per-site reporting is what catches a camera that has drifted. File size and annotation date are not meaningful axes of model behaviour.

questions.stem: What is a confusion matrix most useful for in a multi-class vision problem?
choices: Measuring inference speed
Revealing which specific classes are being mistaken for each other, which often points at a labelling or taxonomy problem rather than a model one
Choosing the learning rate
Counting the dataset size
questions.explanation: A concentrated off-diagonal block tells you far more than an accuracy figure. Two classes consistently confused usually means they are genuinely hard to distinguish, poorly separated in the guideline, or should be merged. Accuracy tells you that errors exist; the matrix tells you what they are.

questions.stem: Your model performs worse on darker skin tones in a face-related task. What is the disciplined response?
choices: Note it as a limitation and ship
Measure performance disaggregated by the affected attribute, identify whether the cause is data coverage, labelling or capture conditions, and rebalance or recollect accordingly before deployment
Increase the model size
Adjust the threshold globally
questions.explanation: Disparate performance is usually a data problem — under-representation, or imaging pipelines tuned for lighter skin — and is fixed at that level. A global threshold change trades error between groups rather than reducing it. Measuring by group is the prerequisite: an aggregate number cannot show the disparity at all.

questions.stem: What is dataset shift, and which variety is most common in deployed vision systems?
choices: The dataset file moving location; storage shift
A change in the input distribution between training and deployment — most often covariate shift from new cameras, lighting, seasons or equipment
A change in the number of classes; label shift only
A change in image format
questions.explanation: The inputs move while the underlying task stays the same: a new camera model, winter light, a repainted production line. Because the labels' meaning is unchanged, the failure is silent — the model simply becomes less accurate with no error raised. Monitoring input statistics is how it is caught.

questions.stem: Why is a benchmark score such as COCO mAP a weak predictor of performance on your application?
choices: Benchmarks are computed incorrectly
It reflects the benchmark's object categories, scales, image quality and scene statistics, which rarely match a specific domain
Benchmarks use different hardware
mAP is not a real metric
questions.explanation: A COCO number says a model is good at internet photographs of eighty everyday categories. Overhead imagery, microscopy, thermal or industrial inspection differ in nearly every relevant respect. Benchmarks rank architectures usefully; they do not predict your accuracy.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices make an evaluation set genuinely useful over time?
choices: Source it from production, weighted toward failures, escalations and edge cases
Keep a held-out slice that is never used for tuning or model selection, so one honest estimate survives
Generate it synthetically from the training distribution
Refresh it to match whatever the model currently does well
questions.explanation: Realism and untouched-ness are what give an evaluation set value. Production sourcing keeps it representative and failure-weighted keeps it difficult; an untouched slice resists the optimism that accumulates from repeated selection. Synthetic data inherits the training distribution's blind spots, and tuning the set to the model inverts the entire purpose.

questions.stem: You have 800 labelled images. Why prefer k-fold cross-validation to a single split?
choices: It trains faster
A single small validation split gives a high-variance estimate; averaging across folds uses all the data for both training and evaluation and gives a more stable number with a spread
It removes the need for a test set
It prevents overfitting
questions.explanation: With 160 validation images, a few unlucky examples move the score by percentage points. Cross-validation reports a mean and a standard deviation, which is what lets you judge whether a difference between two models is real. A final untouched test set is still needed.

questions.stem: Model A scores 0.812 mAP and model B 0.807 on your 400-image test set. What is the right conclusion?
choices: A is better; deploy it
The difference is likely within noise for a set this size; check variance across seeds or folds, and weigh latency, size and failure modes before choosing
B is better because it is simpler
Retrain both for longer
questions.explanation: Half a point on 400 images is a handful of detections and comfortably inside run-to-run variation. Treating it as a real ordering is how teams ship a worse model. When scores are indistinguishable, the tiebreakers should be the practical properties: speed, memory, and how each fails.

questions.stem: What is the value of maintaining a small curated set of known-hard examples?
choices: It replaces the test set
It acts as a regression suite: specific failures that were fixed can be checked cheaply and often, so they cannot silently return
It improves training accuracy
It reduces annotation cost
questions.explanation: A handful of cases that once broke the system — the reflective surface, the occluded pose, the unusual lighting — makes a fast check that runs on every change. It complements rather than replaces a representative test set, which measures overall performance rather than specific known risks.

questions.stem: An object detector's labels were auto-generated by a larger model and then spot-checked. What risk does this create?
choices: No risk if the larger model is accurate
The student inherits the teacher's systematic errors and cannot exceed it on those cases, and spot-checking is unlikely to surface errors that are consistent rather than random
Training will be slower
The labels will be in the wrong format
questions.explanation: Pseudo-labelling is useful but bounds the student by the teacher on any case the teacher gets consistently wrong — and consistent errors are exactly what random spot-checking misses, because they look like agreement. Targeted human review of the teacher's known weak cases is what makes the approach safe.
